DecKeywords: Intervening causes (conduct of worker); Subsequent incidents (outside work); Three week rule (submissions)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a right knee injury in November 1989, which aggravated a preexisting cartilaginous degeneration of the knee. Considering evidence of ongoing medical restrictions and intermittent medical treatment, the Panel found that the 1977 accident, which caused a fairly severe injury, was a significant contributing factor to the ongoing back condition.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (penalty assessments) (improved record); Penalties (accident cost experience)
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming a penalty assessment for the years 1988-1990.

Contrary to the worker's submissions, the evidence of the employer's human resources assistant as to the worker's degree of cooperation in a modified work program was not hearsay.  Her evidence was clear that she was not involved in the initial return to work effort and that she was only able to provide information pertaining to what she observed as a newcomer to the situation.  In any event, the Tribunal is not prohibited from accepting hearsay evidence.

The worker suffered a foot injury in 1966 when a heavy dolly rolled over his steel-toed boot.  He did not lose any time from work.  In 1976, the worker developed hallux rigidus, which means a stiff big toe and is also defined as degenerative arthritis of the first metatarsal phalangeal joint.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement in 1976.

DecKeywords: Alternative employment (comparable employment); Re-employment (non-compliance) (penalty) (mitigation by employer)

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for current back disability which the worker claimed was related to an accident in 1976 when the worker slipped and fell.

DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt; Disablement (change in work); Fibromyalgia; Sewing machine operator
DecSummary: A sewing machine operator appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for neck, right shoulder and low back disability.  The worker began working for the employer in 1979.  In 1981, she was assigned to work on a different machine which required that she sew with her arms raised to chest level.  She complained of pain and, in 1982, changed to a different machine that did not require her to raise her arms.  In 1989, she was assigned to another machine which required that she work standing and with her arms raised to chest level.  She complained of pain and laid off in March 1990.

DecKeywords: Downside risk; Future economic loss {FEL} (calculation); Withdrawal (of appeal)

DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Access Specialist granting the employer access to the worker's file.  The worker was shot in a compensable accident in 1975. The Board granted a 100% pension for psychotraumatic disability.
The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 832/93 was denied.  There was no defect in the process or content of the decision.  [4 pages]

The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 432/93 was denied.  New evidence submitted by the worker was consistent with the worker's position but was based on information provided by the worker many years after the events in question.  Other new evidence also would not have caused the Panel to alter its conclusion.  [5 pages]

The worker appealed Board decisions denying entitlement to a pension for organic back disability and denying entitlement for chronic pain.

The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 735/93 was denied.  [3 pages]

The Board paid dependency benefits to the widow from 1980 to February 1985, and in accordance with s. 37 of the pre-1985 Act, a two-year lump sum on remarriage.  The widow appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying ongoing monthly benefits after February 1985.

The worker suffered a compensable right leg injury in May 1978 and returned to work in June 1978.  She suffered a compensable right ankle injury in October 1984 and returned to work in January 1985.  She was also off work from September 1986 to October 1986 and after November 1986 due to neck, low back and right shoulder conditions which she claimed were related to the accidents in 1978 and 1984 as well as an accident in September 1986.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying reimbursement for the costs incurred in retaining a lawyer to represent him for a Tribunal hearing leading to Decision No. 523/91.
A plumber appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for carpal tunnel syndrome.
The employer withdrew its appeal after two interim decisions had been issued.  The Panel noted with concern the considerable resources that had been expended by the Tribunal on the appeal.  [3 pages]
The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 741/93 was denied.  [3 pages]

DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a pension for hearing loss from exposure to hazardous noise over a period of 25 years. DecKeywords: Procedure (reconsideration) (constitution of Panel); Reconsideration; Right to sue
DecSummary: The defendant in a civil case applied to reconsider Decision No. 847/93 in which the Panel found that the right of action against the defendant was not taken away.

The worker and employer appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer granting reinstatement of vocational rehabilitation services and temporary total disability benefits after January 1993 but denying temporary benefits from September 1992 to January 1993.
The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 18/93 was denied.  [3 pages]

The worker suffered a low back injury in 1970.  He received temporary benefits for various periods until March 1973, when he was awarded a 10% provisional pension for two years.  The worker aggravated his back condition in 1985 while getting out of his car at a Board-sponsored rehabilitation program.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits for the 1985 incident.

The employer appealed a decision that it had not fulfilled its re-employment obligations.  The worker returned to his regular job as a supervisor on an assembly line after his injury.  The day before his injury, the worker had met with his supervisor who told the worker about dissatisfaction with his performance.  A number of the problems indicated to the worker were beyond his control.  The worker's employment was terminated two months after his return to work.  Another supervisor was terminated at the same time.  The worker's supervisor and the plant manager were subsequently terminated, along with a number of other workers.

DecKeywords: Assessment of employers (retroactivity); Board Directives and Guidelines (interest); Discretion, Board (interest); Interest (employer assessment); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board); Merits and justice
DecSummary: The employer was a construction company in the mining contracting business.  It reported payroll to the Board in several different rate groups.  The employer underwent routine audits by the Board in 1982, 1983, and 1986.  There were no recommended changes or reassessments after these audits.  The employer was a member of an industry association which was discussing with the Board the question of how payroll should be assessed where there was interrupted employment.  During these discussions, the Board introduced a new formula for calculating this type of assessment.  The employer group was concerned about an increased cost factor as a result of the new formula, which the Board stated was cost neutral.  It was agreed that the best way to test the formula was to apply it in a real situation.  The employer volunteered to participate in a Board audit to test the effect of the formula.  The Board undertook an extensive special audit in November and December 1988.

DecKeywords: Consequences of injury (residual weakness); Subsequent incidents (outside work)
DecSummary: The worker suffered laceration of two fingers in April 1976 while working with a power saw.  Due to infection, one finger was amputated.  The worker was awarded a 1% pension. The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 844/93 was denied.  [3 pages]

The worker withdrew his appeal after the downside risk of the employers' cross-appeal was explained to the worker.  The employers did not oppose the withdrawal and indicated that they did not intend to pursue the matter further.  [5 pages]

DecKeywords: Exposure (silica dust); Silicosis; Smoking; Mining (gold); Tuberculosis
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision denying him benefits for a respiratory condition.  He worked as an underground gold miner from 1937 to 1944 and from 1949 to 1953.  Board studies and policies acknowledged that gold mines were very dusty at that time, especially pre-1945.  The worker's certificate to work underground was revoked in 1953 due to x-ray evidence of shadowing in his chest.  A workers' compensation claim by the worker was refused in 1954.  At that time, silicosis was not found, but there was evidence of tuberculosis.  The worker was employed above ground from 1953 to 1955, at a wage loss.  From 1955 to 1960, he was receiving active treatment in various sanitaria.  The worker smoked until 1958.

The worker appealed a decision denying him benefits for a urinary tract disability.  In September 1979 the worker was struck by a motor vehicle while he was working.  He was 30 years of age at the time of this accident.  The hospital emergency report indicated that the worker sustained injuries affecting his abdomen, lumbar area, left shoulder, left pelvis, and left knee.  The report stated that the worker experienced pain while producing a urine sample.  The worker testified that he was told by the technician taking the sample that there was some blood in his urine.

DecKeywords: Delay (onset of symptoms); Disablement (strenuous work); Osteoarthritis (wrist)
DecSummary: In June, 1989 the worker fell from a pile of rocks which he was breaking with a sledge hammer.  He was 48 years of age at the time.  The worker initially was treated for a low back injury and he eventually received a 20% pension for his back.  The worker testified that, when he fell from the pile of rocks, he put his hands out behind him to protect his fall.  The worker stated that he felt some pain in his hands and wrists at the time of the accident, but no record was made of complaints of wrist pain at the hospital where the worker was treated.  The worker did not mention his wrists when he was admitted to HRC in February 1990 or when he was examined by an orthopaedic surgeon in March 1990.  He first complained of wrist pain in July 1990.  X-rays and a bone scan performed in November 1990 revealed bilateral old scaphoid bone fractures and advanced degenerative osteoarthritis.
The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue further entitlement at the Board.  [3 pages]

The worker was a deckhand for a shipping company.  He worked with vibratory equipment.  He was awarded a 4% pension for hand-arm vibration syndrome (HAVS).  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits from June 1987 to March 1989 and after May 1991.

The worker started working for the employer in 1988.  In 1991, the plant in which the worker was working was closed for economic reasons.  The employment of 80 workers was terminated but the worker and two others were transferred to another plant.  In May 1992, the worker suffered a compensable injury.  In June 1992, the worker returned to work, at which time he was given notice of termination.  The employer appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding that the employer breached its re-employment obligations.

The worker sustained a compensable contusion injury to his knee in January 1974 with possible twisting.  A torn medial meniscus was suspected and a menisectomy was performed in March 1974.  In August 1982 the worker sustained a compensable low back sprain while cutting trees with a chain saw.  The worker claimed that  he suffered a new accident in October 1987.  The worker appealed the denial of further benefits for his back and knee.
The worker suffered a crush injury to his hand in August 1987.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying VR and supplementary benefits after December 1991.

DecKeywords: Chronic pain; Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (evidence to support Appeal Board conclusion); Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (medical report)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a right knee injury in 1972.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for chronic pain and applied for leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board denying benefits in 1977 for organic or psychological disability.

A truck driver who operated a trucking business suffered a fractured leg in 1984, for which he was awarded a 50% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for psychotraumatic disability.
The worker suffered a back injury in May 1991.  The worker appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer denying benefits and vocational rehabilitation assistance after November 1991.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer and applied for leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board regarding accidents in 1979 and 1981.  On the evidence, the Panel found that the accident in 1981 was a recurrence of the 1979 disability rather than a new accident.  Given this finding, it was not necessary for the worker to pursue the leave to appeal issue.
In Decisions No. 749/93I and 749/93I2, the Panel referred the case back to the Board for an assessment of the worker on a whole person basis.

A firefighter was on a roof fighting a residential fire, when he reached out to grab a falling co-worker.  He felt pain across the top of his chest, which he thought to be a muscle strain.  Thirty-three hours later, the worker suffered a heart attack while sleeping in the fire station.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for the heart attack.

A 67 year old worker was struck by a car in a minor compensable accident in 1988.  The initial diagnosis was left arm and buttock contusion.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for diabetes and a number of other conditions.

DecKeywords: Cancer (lung); Industrial Disease Standards Panel (nickel); Mining (nickel); Reconsideration (consideration of evidence)
DecSummary: The Chair of the Industrial Disease Standards Panel applied for reconsideration of Decision No. 199/93L.  In Decision No. 199/93L, the hearing panel denied the application of the worker's widow for leave to appeal denial of entitlement for the worker's death from lung cancer.  The Chair of the IDSP submitted that the hearing panel mischaracterized a document on which the application was based.

The worker suffered a chest wall injury in July 1981.  She received temporary benefits until August 1981.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further temporary benefits and denying a pension.
The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 98/93L was denied.  There was no significant defect in the original decision.  [4 pages]

The worker's widow claimed entitlement to survivor's benefits under the pre-1985 Act.  The claimant and the worker were married in Jamaica and had four children there.  In 1970 the worker separated from the claimant.  He moved to Canada in 1973 and died in a work-related accident in 1975.  The Board determined that the children of the marriage were dependants under the Act who were thus entitled to benefits, but that the claimant was not a dependant.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a low back injury which he claimed he suffered on his first day of work at the accident employer while he was being initiated to his duties by the lead hand.
A s. 17 application was withdrawn.  The matter had been settled and the defendant applicant no longer had reason to proceed.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Availability for employment (refusing suitable work); Rehabilitation, vocational (cooperation)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a right wrist injury in a fall in 1987, for which he was awarded a 4% pension.  The worker returned to work for one day in June 1990 and tried a number of different jobs.  The next day, the worker met with the Board's caseworker, the employer's plant manager and the union president.  It was suggested that the worker participate in a transitional work hardening program but the worker did not feel that a gradual increase in hours would help.  The Board found that the worker was entitled to temporary partial disability benefits since the jobs offered were not suitable for the worker.  The employer appealed.
The worker felt pain in his back, neck and shoulders while lifting a heavy object at work in May 1989.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for chronic pain.

The worker injured his back at work in May 1987 when he had to support a 60 to 70 pound weight over his head with his back in a flexed, hyperextended position.  He experienced pain in his low back which radiated down to his leg.  The worker received various periods of temporary benefits until he was awarded a 15% pension in December 1989.  However, in a 1992 decision, the worker was denied benefits for neck and arm problems which he related to the same accident.  The worker appealed this decision.

DecKeywords: Contractor (principal's liability for assessments); Corporation (piercing corporate veil)
DecSummary: The employer was a timber broker.  It contracted with others for cutting, hauling and processing timber.  These contracts were usually with related companies.  The Board found the employer liable for the WCB indebtedness of the related companies under s. 11(3), as a principal responsible for the compensation liability of its contractors.  The Board also found that the related companies were so closely associated that they were really one single entity.  As such, the Board pierced the corporate veil and found the employer liable for the debts of the other companies.  The employer appealed.

DecKeywords: Arising out of employment (common activity); In the course of employment (off duty)
DecSummary: The worker attended a staff meeting on her day off. While bending over to adjust her chair, the worker sneezed and experienced back pain.  The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement.

DecSummary: The worker fell 25 feet from a scaffold in December 1965.  The worker's widow appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for psychotraumatic disability.

DecSummary: The worker sustained a serious injury in March 1971. In August 1991, the worker made a bid under his union contract for a temporary job as a flagman.  He worked as a flagman until the end of October 1991 when that job was no longer available.  The employer then would not let the worker return to his regular job as a trackman until he obtained medical clearance, as there was concern over his ability to perform regular work.  The employer appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding that the employer breached its re-employment obligations and levying a penalty of the maximum allowed.

There were varying diagnoses for the worker's condition, including bursitis, non-organic disability, rotator cuff tendinitis and torn acromioclavicular meniscus.

The employer appealed a decision of the Reinstatement Officer finding that it breached its re-employment obligations.

DecSummary: The defendants in a civil case applied to determine whether the plaintiffs' civil right of action was taken away.  The issue was the status of the plaintiffs at the time of a motor vehicle accident.

DecKeywords: Corporation (piercing corporate veil); Independent operator (owner/operator); Worker (deemed)
DecSummary: The employer was a company in the business of loading and hauling timber.  Some of its work was carried out by owner/operators.  In 1987, it adopted a policy of only contracting with incorporated owner/operators.  Most of its owner/operators were already incorporated prior to 1987.  Three owner/operators incorporated after announcement of the policy.  The Board decided that the owner/operators who incorporated after 1987 did so on the basis of the employer's requirement, in order to avoid paying workers' compensation premiums for those owner/operators.  The Hearings Officer concluded that those owner/operators were workers within the meaning of the Act.  The employer appealed.
The worker suffered a shoulder and elbow injury while lifting a heavy object at work in April 1984.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits after January 1985.

DecKeywords: Adjournment (additional medical evidence); Investigation by Tribunal
DecSummary: The worker struck his low back in 1983 when standing up from a crawling position.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a prolapsed disc in 1987.  The Panel required additional expert medical evidence before it could make a decision.  The Panel made findings of fact and directed that the opinion of a Tribunal assessor be obtained on a number of medical issues based on these findings of fact.

DecKeywords: Reconsideration (amendment of decision); Re-employment (duration of obligation)
DecSummary: On application of the worker and employer, one aspect of Decision No. 605/93I2 was reconsidered.  In Decision No. 605/93I2, the Panel found that the duration of the obligation to re-employ under s. 54(8)(a) lasted until December 1992, which was two years from the date of the injury.  However, the worker returned to pre-injury employment in June 1991.  Accordingly, s. 54(8)(b) was applicable, and the obligation to re-employ lasted for one year, until June 1992.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for low back disability after July 1988, which the worker related to compensable accidents in 1974, 1976, 1977, 1978 and 1980.  On the evidence, the worker was suffering from degenerative disc disease.  The compensable accidents did not trigger, aggravate or accelerate the normal aging process.

DecKeywords: Maximal medical rehabilitation; Temporary disability (beyond pension level)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a left shoulder injury in 1977 for which she was awarded a 15% pension.  In February 1986, she had a recurrence and was awarded temporary disability benefits until January 1988.  In January 1990, the worker underwent shoulder surgery.  She received temporary benefits from January 1990 until her return to work in 1992.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits from January 1988 to January 1990.

The worker suffered a right knee injury in January 1986 and received benefits until May 1986.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits subsequent to May 1986.

The worker fell, striking his head.  He had a seizure two days later and another seizure five months later.  The Board originally granted benefits for post-traumatic epilepsy but later reversed that decision.  The worker appealed denial of benefits for the seizure disorder.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (health care) (out of province); Medical treatment (special); Out of province (health care)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a neck injury in 1985 and underwent a discectomy and fusion at C5-6 in 1986.  The worker continued to have neck symptoms.  Further surgery was not recommended until the worker had MRI scan.  However, doctors were reluctant to organize the MRI and there would be a wait of at least one year.  The worker was referred to an orthopaedic surgeon in Buffalo.  The MRI was done in Buffalo within a few weeks.  Surgery was performed in Buffalo in 1990 and 1991.  The Board reimbursed the worker for 75% of the cost.  The worker appealed the decision of the Hearings Officer denying full reimbursement.

The worker suffered a cervical injury in 1979 for which he was awarded a 25% pension.  The worker was also granted health care benefits for chiropractic treatment twice per month.  The worker appealed denial of an increase in the frequency of chiropractic treatment and denial of entitlement for a low back disability.

DecKeywords: Asthma; Consequences of injury (stress, mental); Exposure (isocyanate fumes) (toluene diisocyanate); Glottal dysfunction syndrome
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision confirming the worker's entitlement to benefits for occupational asthma resulting from the worker's employment.  The worker was employed in a plant which manufactured polyurethane foam.

DecKeywords: Continuity (of complaint); Evidence (testimony from Hearings Officer decision); Recurrences (compensable injury)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a back injury in August 1987 and returned to regular work in January 1988.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a recurrence in November 1988.
The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to return to the Board and request reconsideration of the Board decision on the basis of significant new evidence.  [4 pages]

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming 50% temporary partial disability benefits for the period in question.  The Panel identified the issues on the appeal as whether the worker was temporarily disabled during the period, and if so, whether the disability was total or partial, and if partial, whether there was entitlement to full benefits.

DecKeywords: Independent operator (courier); Notice of hearing; Transportation industry (courier); Worker (test) (business reality)
DecSummary: The employer was a courier company.  Originally, the employer had been classified as a dispatch service.  Following an audit in 1983, the Board ruled that the employer was a courier service but that its broker-drivers were independent operators.  After an accident involving one of the broker-drivers in 1988, the Board conducted another survey of the employer's status and found that the broker-drivers were workers under the Act.  This order was made effective January 1988.  In 1992, the Board started reviewing the status of the broker-drivers using the organizational test that the Board recently adopted.  The employer appealed the decision of the Hearings Officer confirming the status of the broker-drivers as workers for the period from 1988 to 1992.

DecKeywords: Continuity (of symptoms); Credibility (delay); Earnings basis (recurrences); Health care (clothing allowance)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back strain in November 1960 and received benefits until June 1961.  In 1979, he underwent surgery for a herniated disc.  The Board granted benefits for the surgery.  The worker also was awarded a 20% pension in 1984 and a clothing allowance in 1987.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits for three periods in 1961 and 1962, denying an increase in the pension, denying a clothing allowance from 1961 to 1987 and calculating the worker's benefits in 1979 on the basis of his escalated pre-accident earnings.

DecKeywords: Reconsideration (consideration of evidence); Right to sue
DecSummary: An application to reconsider Decision No. 351/93 was denied.  [4 pages]

The worker appealed the decision of the Hearings Officer denying further increase in the pension.

DecKeywords: Continuing entitlement; Medical report (varying diagnoses); Preexisting condition (hyperostosis)
DecSummary: The worker fell 15 feet from a ladder in 1981, injuring his tailbone and lower back.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for lower thoracic and right subcostal pain in 1985.

DecKeywords: Permanent disability; Supplements, older worker; Supplements, transitional provisions (permanent) (duration); Temporary disability (beyond pension level)

The worker claimed that he advised his foreman on December 21, 1990 that he had felt pain in his shoulder while pushing a rack of tires.  The foreman testified that the worker first advised him of the incident in January 1991, after the Christmas shutdown.  The foreman testified that the worker told him he had been cutting firewood during the shutdown.  The worker denied this.  The worker stopped working, due to his shoulder condition, in February 1990.

DecKeywords: Supplements, temporary; Supplements, transitional provisions (benefit from rehabilitation)

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying supplementary benefits after July 1989.

An autopsy determined the cause of death to be chronic obstructive lung disease with acute pneumonia and end stage kidneys.  The worker's widow appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits for the worker's death.

DecKeywords: Disablement (nature of work); Postal workers (letter carrier)
DecSummary: A letter carrier appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for low back disability which he related to the nature of his work.  On the evidence, the Panel found that the worker had underlying degenerative disc disease which was symptomatic periodically but which was not symptomatic immediately prior to the onset of symptoms in question.  The worker's job was physically demanding and put stress on his back.  The Panel concluded that the symptoms of the worker's degenerative disc disease were aggravated by his employment activities but that the employment activities did not aggravate the actual degenerative process.

The employer's application to require the worker to attend a medical examination was adjourned to allow the employer to review new medical evidence of which it was unaware.  The employer would then inform the Tribunal whether it would proceed with or withdraw the application.  [3 pages]
The worker suffered a foot injury in 1987 for which he was awarded a 1% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits from October 1990 to February 1991.

The Panel was concerned that the worker may not fully appreciate the appeal process.

The plan was that the worker would start off working two hours per day which would then be increased to four hours.  The worker stopped working after one week without progressing to four hour days.  The issue was whether the worker refused suitable work.

DecKeywords: Damages, contribution or indemnity; Right to sue (third party claims)
DecSummary: The third party in a civil case applied for an order that the defendant has no right to recover damages, contribution or indemnity against it connection with the action.  The plaintiff was a worker of the third party.  The plaintiff was injured when the bucket on a bucket truck fell to the ground.  The plaintiff commenced the action against the defendant, which had been retained by the third party to service the truck.  The defendant brought the third party proceedings alleging that the plaintiff's injuries resulted from negligence of the plaintiff and the third party.

DecKeywords: Disablement (repetitive work); Office worker (secretary); Osteoarthritis (hand); Significant contribution (of employment to disability)
DecSummary: A 63 year old secretary appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for bilateral osteoarthritis of the hands. For about 25 of those years, she used a manual typewriter.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Rehabilitation program (particulars of program) (work trial)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a left knee injury in August 1991.  In March 1992, the worker returned to modified work in accordance with a vocational rehabilitation plan that was agreed upon by the worker, the employer and the Board caseworker.  The plan called for an eight week work trial with medical restrictions.  The worker missed some days of work during the work trial.  The caseworker interpreted this as a refusal to continue the work trial.  The worker's rehabilitation file was closed and benefits were terminated.  The worker appealed.

The worker appealed a decision denying benefits for an epileptic condition which manifested itself within days of an alleged unwitnessed accident at work.  The worker claimed that he experienced a blackout episode after he struck his head against a pipe as he stood up, in September 1988.  The worker was involved in motor vehicle accidents in March 1987 and July 1987, the second of which caused a bump on the head.

The worker fractured his right hand in 1976.  He was awarded a 5% pension in 1978.  In March 1983, the worker had surgery to remove a ganglion (a fluid filled swelling or cyst on a tendon) on his right wrist.  The worker received benefits for this as of March 1983.  The worker appealed denial of benefits for the ganglion from January 1982 to March 1983.
The worker suffered knee injuries in 1979 and 1980.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further benefits in 1989.

He wanted a comprehensive review of his pension level, taking into account the combined effect of the two disabilities.

DecKeywords: Intervening causes; Significant contribution (of compensable accident to disability); Subsequent incidents (outside work)

DecKeywords: Angina pectoris; Heart attack; Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board); Medical opinion (angina pectoris) (stress); Preexisting condition (coronary artery disease)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a heart attack in February 1989 after unusual exertion.  The Board granted benefits on an aggravation basis.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for angina and fatigue.  In Decision No. 367/93I, the Panel found that Cardizem was used to treat the angina, and that the Cardizem caused swelling.  Lasix was then used to treat the swelling, and this led to the fatigue.  The issue then became whether the angina was compensable.

A carpenter was crawling under a scaffold in September 1983.  He struck his back against a pipe as he moved to stand up.  He was off work for one week.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a prolapsed disc in 1987, which the worker claimed was related to the accident in 1983.

He was also awarded a 10% pension for impotence which was related to the compensable accident.  The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying entitlement for psychotraumatic disability.

DecKeywords: Adjournment (referral to Board); Procedure (expedited WCB decision requested)
DecSummary: In Decision No. 169/93I, the hearing was adjourned and the matter referred to the Board for a final decision on a number of issues, so that the matter could be dealt with on a whole person basis. The Board closed his rehabilitation file and terminated his benefits after finding that the job was suitable.  A FEL assessment was done in which it was found that the worker was not entitled to a FEL award since he had been offered suitable employment at no wage loss.

In Decision No. 501/89, a different panel found that the worker was entitled to temporary benefits for organic disability until October 1984.  That panel was only considering entitlement for organic disability, but noted that the worker may be suffering from non-organic disability.  The worker sought entitlement from the Board for non-organic disability. A miner suffered injuries in 1970, 1972, 1975 and 1976.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for low back disability in 1986.

The hearing was adjourned to allow the worker to return to the Board to pursue entitlement for chronic pain.  [3 pages]

The worker received benefits on an aggravation basis for spondylolisthesis in 1979.  The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying future entitlement to benefits.

The Board paid benefits from May 1986 to September 1986, but discontinued them on the basis that the worker no longer had a compensable disability.  The worker continued to complain of low back pain radiating into her leg and of shoulder pain.  She claimed temporary benefits from September 1986 to October 1987 when she returned to her regular job as a sewing machine operator for a period.

DecSummary: While trying to board a moving train, the worker's shoulder was yanked.  He was awarded a 15% pension for shoulder disability.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for neck disability which the worker claimed he also suffered in the compensable accident.

DecSummary: The worker suffered a non-compensable tear of his anterior cruciate ligament in 1986.  In August 1987, he suffered a torn meniscus in a compensable accident.  In September 1987, he underwent surgery to correct both conditions.  He received benefits on an aggravation basis until January 1988.  In September 1988, the worker was playing catch at home when his knee gave out, again rupturing the ligament and tearing the meniscus.  He underwent surgery again to reconstruct the ligament and suture the meniscus.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for the incident in September 1988.

DecKeywords: Consequences of injury (altered gait); Psychotraumatic disability
DecSummary: The worker suffered a comminuted fracture of the left femur in September 1981, for which he was awarded a 25% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying full temporary benefits from April 1983 to January l984 and denying entitlement for left knee, low back and psychological disability.

DecKeywords: Agreement (parties); Medical examination (employer request); Withdrawal (of application)
DecSummary: The employer withdrew its application to require the worker to attend a medical examination after the worker agreed to give the employer copies of new medical reports to which the employer had not received access.  [3 pages]

P Ltd also retained the services of drivers who owned their own tractors and trailers for the purpose of hauling aggregate.  For drivers who only owned a tractor, but no trailer, N Ltd provided the trailer and the owner/operator was retained by N Ltd.  The issue before this Panel was whether the owner/operators associated with P Ltd and N Ltd, who did not own their own trailers, were workers or independent operators under the Act, for the period between January 1987 and December 1991.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for bilateral chondromalacia patella which the worker related to the repetitive nature of her work.  Considering the height of the worker's work station and the worker's description and demonstration of her work activities, the Panel found that the worker did not suffer repetitive trauma to her knees.  She did not repetitively bang her knees against the assembly line where she worked.  The Panel concluded that the worker's knee condition was not related to the nature of her employment.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (issue in dispute) (SIEF); Access to worker file, statutory (non-medical information); Board Directives and Guidelines (access to worker file, statutory) (non-medical information)
DecSummary: The employer appealed two decisions of the Access Specialist.  The first denied the employer access to the worker's prior claim files which the employer argued were required to support its claim for SIEF relief.  The second denied the employer access to a non-medical document which the employer argued was relevant to the issue of ongoing entitlement.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (issue in dispute) (relevance)
DecSummary: Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer except for a paragraph in a psychiatric report concerning the worker's earlier life experiences before her immigration to Canada.

The employer's appeal and the worker's cross-appeal were withdrawn on a joint request.  Because of the considerable resources which have gone into preparation of this case, and because the hearing had not proceeded on two separate days, the matter will not be permitted to be brought back unless it has been reviewed by a panel of the Tribunal.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Continuing entitlement; Consequences of injury (residual weakness); Construction (bricklayer); Disablement (nature of work)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision denying him ongoing entitlement, after September 1990, for a back condition which he related to: a compensable low back strain in July 1977, a compensable knee injury in September 1987 and/or the general nature of his employment as a bricklayer.

The worker's appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to obtain final decisions from the Board on all areas of entitlement and all related issues flowing from the decisions concerning areas of entitlement.  [5 pages]

DecKeywords: Consequences of injury; Chronic obstructive lung disease
DecSummary: The worker suffered a shoulder strain in 1966.  The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying entitlement for a respiratory condition which the worker claimed resulted from inhalation of smoke and chemicals during a fire at HRC in 1967.

The worker suffered a low back injury when she tripped and fell backwards, landing on her buttocks, in February 1989.  The worker did not claim benefits until April 1991.  The Hearings Officer granted health care benefits only, but denied entitlement for lost time or for further treatment subsequent to January 1991.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [3 pages]

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (penalty assessments) (improved record); Discretion, Board (employer assessment) (fettering); Merits and justice; Penalties (level of penalty)

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (supplements, transitional provisions) (temporary) (participation in rehabilitation); Supplements, transitional provisions (temporary) (participation in rehabilitation)
DecSummary: The worker was a painter who suffered an ankle injury in a fall in 1984, for which he was awarded a pension.  The worker received supplementary benefits until July 1989, when his rehabilitation file was closed.  The Hearings Officer found that the worker was entitled to further rehabilitation assistance after July 1991.  The worker appealed denial of a s. 147(2) supplement from July 1989 to July 1991.

DecKeywords: Issue setting; Jurisdiction, Board (decision of Tribunal); Reconsideration (clarification of decision)
DecSummary: The Board requested that the Tribunal clarify Decision No. 489/93I.  The Board was unclear as to whether the hearing panel's reference to an attempted return to work in March 1993 operated so as to deprive the Board of jurisdiction to hear a matter which addressed the events of that date.  The Board asked whether the Tribunal's decision effectively addressed the issue of return to work and thereby deprived the Board of jurisdiction to decide it.

The worker was a 58 year old steel plant worker in 1990, when a vessel erupted and ejected particles of hot metal.  He suffered superficial burns to his back and ankle.  The worker complained of hearing loss, frontal headaches, ringing in his ears, and dizziness.  He did not lose time from work.  The worker retired from work in 1991.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for hearing loss.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  [4 pages]

The worker suffered a low back injury for which he was awarded a 15% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying an increase in the pension.  The worker submitted that  the pension failed to reflect the presence of chronic pain and failed to reflect the extent of organic disability.

DecKeywords: Anxiety; Psychotraumatic disability; Permanent disability; Tachycardia (ventricular)
DecSummary: In April 1984, the worker suffered an episode of supraventricular tachycardia (abnormally rapid heart rate).  After lengthy adjudication and intervention by the Ombudsman, the Board granted entitlement for aggravation of a preexisting condition until March 1985.  The worker appealed denial of entitlement to a pension.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for surgical repair of an inguinal hernia in December 1991.  The worker claimed that he suffered the hernia in a compensable accident in 1982 or 1987.

The defendant in a civil case applied to determine whether the plaintiff's right of action was taken away.  The plaintiff did not oppose the application.  The Panel found that the plaintiff was a worker of a Schedule 1 employer who was assigned to work at the defendant's premises.  An accident occurred in the course of the worker's employment.  There were workers of the defendant who were also in the course of employment at the time of the accident.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (medical report)
DecSummary: The worker applied for leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board denying entitlement subsequent to November 1977 for a condition which the worker claimed was related to an accident in 1976.  The worker submitted a new medical report dated in 1992.  The Panel found that the medical report did not constitute substantial new evidence since it was not substantially different from other medical reports on file.  Further, it was not likely that a different decision would have been reached had the report been available.

DecKeywords: Earnings basis (learner); Earnings basis (nominal remuneration); Earnings basis (short or casual employment); Impairment of earning capacity; Significantly greater than is usual; Supplements, temporary
DecSummary: The worker was injured six days after he started work in a building supply store in October 1981.  He was awarded a 15% pension. DecKeywords: Adjournment (additional issues); Issue setting; Three week rule (documents)
DecSummary: The worker was appealing a decision of the Hearings Officer.  The Case Description described the issue as being entitlement to supplementary benefits subsequent to January 1992.  The Panel found that the issue was entitlement to benefits subsequent to January 1992.  This required a determination of whether the worker had achieved maximal medical rehabilitation.  If not, it then had to be decided whether the worker was entitled to temporary benefits, based on the criteria in s. 37.  If the worker had achieved maximal medical rehabilitation, it had to be decided whether his pension level was correct and whether he was entitled to a supplement.

The worker suffered avulsion of the tip of his thumb and amputation of part of his index finger in a compensable accident in 1966.  He was awarded a 3% pension (2% for the finger and 1% for the thumb).  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming the amount of the pension.

The worker suffered a low back strain in July 1984 and a recurrence in November 1984.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement subsequent to August 1985.

The employer applied for an order requiring the worker to attend a medical examination by a doctor selected by the employer.  The worker was planning to appeal a Board decision denying entitlement for elbow disability.  An examination by an orthopaedic surgeon selected by the employer found that the orthopaedic problem was minor but that there might be other factors, such as psychological problems, which prevented the worker from working.  The employer then requested that the worker attend an examination by a psychiatrist.  The worker refused and the employer brought this application.

The worker was appealing confirmation of a 20% pension for organic shoulder disability.  In Decision No. 756/93I, the Panel referred the matter back to the Board for a further pension examination.  The Board doctor again confirmed the 20% award.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (commutation); Commutation; Delay (appeal); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board) (commutation)
DecSummary: The Panel denied the worker's request for a commutation of his pension.  As there was no clear rehabilitative purpose, the request was contrary to the Board's current policy.  To depart from Board policy a well-conceived and fully-researched proposal would be required.  This worker's commutation request was extremely vague.  The worker's representative said that the commutation was required to pay off debts.  The worker testified that he would pay off a bank loan, but most of the proceeds would go to home repair and an RRSP contribution.

The worker suffered a low back and knee injury in a fall in December 1988.  He was awarded a 20% pension for chronic pain in June 1991.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting only 50% benefits for temporary partial disability from November 1990 to June 1991.

The worker suffered a low back injury in September 1989.  She returned to work from February 1990 to May 1990.  She received temporary total disability benefits from May 1990 to June 1990 and 50% temporary partial disability benefits from June 1990 to July 1990.  In October 1992, the Hearings Officer found that the worker was also entitled to benefits for aggravation of preexisting fibromyalgia but was not entitled to further temporary benefits.  The worker appealed the decision of the Hearings Officer denying further temporary benefits.

DecSummary: The worker was injured at work in September 1983 and received benefits for a disability that involved back, groin and leg pain.  He returned to work in January 1984 but he continued to receive medical treatment for pain in his back, chest, arm, shoulders and neck, as well as for hypertension.  After applying for early retirement from his employer, the worker sustained another injury in July 1985.  He subsequently sought treatment for neck, shoulder, back and leg pain.  The worker retired from the accident employer's workforce in September 1985 and he had not looked for work since the July 1985 accident.  He was currently receiving pensions totalling 29% as a result of compensable accidents.

DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision denying him a pension for an asthma condition which he developed while employed by a company that produced foam seats for automobiles.  He was exposed to toluene diisocyanates in that job.  The worker started working with that employer in January 1985 and stopped in March 1985.  He was awarded a two-year provisional pension that expired in February 1989. The worker injured his knee at work in 1982.  He was awarded a 5% pension in 1984.  The worker returned to his former job as a truck driver in 1984 and sustained a second injury to the same knee in 1986.  The worker was paid temporary benefits after the 1986 injury but the Board determined that he had not sustained a permanent injury as a result of that accident.  The worker sought pension benefits for knee injuries sustained in the 1986 accident.
The appeal was adjourned and the matter referred to the Board for final adjudication of a number of issues, so that the case could be heard on a whole person basis.  [7 pages]

DecKeywords: Interest; Overpayment; Temporary disability (beyond pension level)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a compensable accident in 1980 for which she was awarded a 10% pension.  In 1984, she was awarded a full supplement.  Although she notified the Board that she obtained employment, the Board continued to pay the supplement.  In 1987, she received temporary benefits for a recurrence from May to August.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying temporary benefits from August 1987 to September 1987 and directing repayment of the overpayment of the supplement.

The employer withdrew its application for an order requiring the worker to attend a medical examination after the worker consented to release of a number of medical reports to which the employer had not had access.  [3 pages]

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a back disability.  On the evidence, the Panel found that the worker did not perform strenuous work on a regular basis but that he did perform strenuous work during one week in October 1989.  The worker's condition resulted from that strenuous work.  The worker may have had a preexisting degenerative condition but, if so, the preexisting condition was asymptomatic until triggered by the strenuous work.

DecKeywords: Adjournment (Board submissions); Board Directives and Guidelines (supplements, transitional provisions) (wage loss)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a compensable back injury in 1979 for which he was awarded a 20% pension.  He moved to British Columbia and worked until 1982 when he had another accident.  The worker was appealing a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a supplement under s. 147(4).
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer, except for a number of references which were not relevant.  [5 pages]

The worker suffered a back injury while carrying supplies in October 1989.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement after January 1990.  On the evidence, the accident was minor.  It aggravated a significant preexisting back condition.  However, the aggravation was temporary.  The accident was not a significant contributing factor to the worker's current condition.

The worker was appealing denial of benefits in 1988 for a back condition which he related to compensable accidents in 1975 and 1987.  The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue entitlement on the basis of disablement from the nature of his work.

DecKeywords: Hearing loss; Medical opinion (hearing loss) (deterioration after removal from exposure); Overpayment
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement for hearing loss.  The worker worked for the accident employer for 26 years.  He retired in 1979.  An audiogram in 1976 showed hearing loss of 11 decibels in the left ear and 10 decibels in the right ear.  Another audiogram in 1979 showed hearing loss of 15 decibels in the left ear and 13 in the right ear.  Entitlement was based on an audiogram in 1986 showing hearing loss of 35 decibels in the left ear and 25 decibels in the right ear.

The worker appealed a decision entitling him to only 50% temporary benefits.  Despite his low academic functioning, the worker insisted on receiving retraining and did not perform a job search in the sales area as recommended by Board vocational rehabilitation caseworkers.  The worker was suffering from psychiatric symptoms, but the issue of whether the compensable accident was a significant contributing factor to these symptoms or to the worker's addiction conditions was not before the Panel.

DecKeywords: Parties (interest of worker) (SIEF); Second Injury and Enhancement Fund {SIEF} (preexisting condition)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting 75% SIEF relief to the employer for a knee injury suffered by the worker. DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (issue in dispute) (interest of employer); Parties (interest of worker)
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision of the Claims Services Division denying access to the worker's file.  The Board had found that the worker had work related hearing loss but that the degree of loss was insufficient to warrant an award and that, therefore, the award would be 0%.  The employer was appealing the conclusion that the hearing loss was work related.  The worker had not appealed the decision.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, P. D.; Adjournment (issue splitting); Adjournment (preparation)
DecSummary: The employer was appealing a decision of the Hearings Officer in February 1992 restoring rehabilitations services and a supplement subsequent to March 1991.  The employer submitted that it should be given access to material in the worker's file pertaining to developments subsequent to the date of the Hearings Officer's decision.  The Panel agreed that the employer should have access since the worker's conduct and cooperation after being eligible for assistance may go to the intent of the worker in requesting the assistance.

The worker was appealing denial of a s. 147(4) supplement.  The worker had never been assessed by the vocational rehabilitation staff at the Board.  The Panel could not make a determination without an assessment by the Board as to the likelihood of the worker benefiting from a vocational rehabilitation plan.

The worker was appealing a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for foot and low back disability resulting from her work as a cashier.  The Hearings Officer did not consider entitlement for arm and shoulder disability also resulting from her work.

DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision of the Technical Adviser, Experience Rating, which denied it the right to appeal the issue of the method used by the Board to implement the 'best of three' formula under the NEER rating system. On the evidence, modified work that the worker tried for one day in May 1990 was not suitable.  He was cooperating with rehabilitation.  He was entitled to full temporary partial disability benefits during the period in question.

DecSummary: T's widow appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying dependency benefits for T's death from a heart attack.  T was the sole shareholder of a T Trucking. The worker appealed decisions of the Hearings Officer denying a pension for the elbow condition, denying entitlement for lymph gland problems and denying entitlement for psychological disability.

A patio flagstone fell against the the worker's thigh while she was standing in a twisted position.  The front of her waist was thrown against the handle of a cart.  The worker sustained contusions to the left thigh and hip region for which she received benefits from June 1988 to September 1988.  The worker sought benefits for subsequent periods based on the development of low back and neck pain which she related to the accident.  The worker also was eventually diagnosed as having fibromyalgia.
The appeal was withdrawn to allow the worker to pursue additional issues at the Board.  [3 pages]

In April 1990, the worker got new work boots from his employer.  Since his size was not available, he took a smaller size.  The worker, who was diabetic, developed an ulceration of the toe, requiring debridement.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting only 50% temporary benefits from October 1991 to January 1992 and denying entitlement to a FEL award.

The worker suffered a low back injury in 1988.  In January 1991, he was awarded a 20%  two-year provisional pension for chronic pain.  The worker appealed denial of an increase in the pension, denial of vocational rehabilitation services after February 1991 and denial of full temporary benefits from March 1991 to May 1991.

The hearing was adjourned to obtain up-to-date medical evidence which both parties felt was necessary.  The issue was the level of temporary benefits between November 1991 and March 1993.  There were no medical reports on file concerning the worker's back condition since May 1992.  The Panel directed that a copy of the Board's assessment of the worker's back disability, conducted in March 1993, be obtained and that more information be requested from the worker's family doctor with respect to the period after May 1992.  [4 pages]

Although there was a delay in onset of recorded neck symptoms until the 1970s, the Panel found that the worker suffered a neck injury in the accident.

The worker slipped at work on October 27 and experienced back pain.  He did not seek medical attention until November 2.  At that time, he attributed his condition to the heavier nature of his work at a new construction site rather than the incident on October 27, which he considered to be minor.  Later, he attributed the condition to the slip.  The Panel found that this and other inconsistencies were not significant.

DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for ankylosing spondylitis in April 1988 which the worker claimed was related to a compensable neck injury in March 1985 or to the nature of his work in February 1988.

DecSummary: The worker applied for an order that she was not required to attend a medical examination requested by the employer.
